cells.tense: You are here, with the pen, at a release already underway.
cells.act: make the fair call about a feeling, yourself
cells.ask: When a feeling comes up about something you're setting down, make the call yourself — what it deserves, what it gets — and don't run it past anyone.
cells.core:
You can tell what's finished and what still needs holding, and you don't have to make a case for it. Things leave your life cleanly because the call is right: you set down the part that's done, you keep what's still worth carrying, and the difference between the two is steady rather than worked out each time. People watching you release something see it come apart without a fuss. The ground stays under you.

Where this goes next is fairness toward yourself. Pick something you've meant to set down and make the call about it alone — what it costs you, what it gives, what it gets from here. No second opinion, no rehearsal. If it's time, it's time; if it isn't, say so to yourself and mean it. The clear call is the whole act. What follows is lighter because you didn't ask permission from anyone, including from your own old reasons.
cells.sheetLine: You can let go and keep what still matters, at once.

cells.tense: You are bracing at a future where the release has not happened yet.
cells.act: hold space for what someone feels without fixing it
cells.ask: Next time someone tells you what they feel, don't fix it, don't explain it, don't hand them a next step. Stay with it until they're done, and then stay a beat longer.
cells.core:
What's over is being kept past its time, and keeping it doesn't move your hands any closer to setting it down. There is a version of this that's finished, and you're holding it warm for some future where it turns out to have been worth keeping. So you feed what should be composted, and that feeding gets heavier each time. The shelf where finished things go has stopped being cleared.

Come back through other people. The next person who comes to you with something they feel — let it be theirs. Don't fix it, don't explain it, don't hand them the next step. Stay with it until they finish, and then a beat longer than is comfortable. What you're doing for them is the thing you're refusing to do about your own ending. The release doesn't happen tonight. But the grip eases when you stop holding their feelings together.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding something warm that's already done.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that has already closed behind you.
cells.act: feed the drive a little at a time
cells.ask: Choose one easy thing you already want to do — not a big decision — and do it today. Then again tomorrow. Don't wait to feel ready.
cells.core:
The setting-down isn't happening here. What should have left is still around, and the space is quieter because of it — not because you're gripping hard, but because you stopped reaching for the handle. Your hand is back where things used to be. Work that never got finished sits where you can see it and you walk past without picking anything up or putting anything down.

Don't try to feel your way back. The way back is through your own want, given in small amounts. Choose one easy thing you already want to do, something with no weight on it, and do it today. Then again tomorrow. Don't wait to feel like it. Wanting catches up to doing, not the other way around. You aren't behind. You're standing still, and doing one easy thing moves you.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped reaching for the handle, and the room got quiet.

cells.tense: You are at a release already happening, and calling it circumstance.
cells.act: cut through the inertia with one decisive act
cells.ask: Take something you're already setting down and do the one act that puts it outside your head — send the message, clear the shelf, settle the account. One act, today.
cells.core:
You are already setting something down — clearing it out, making room, changing the terms — and if someone asked, you'd say it just happened. It didn't. You made the call, and the call was sound, and the soundness of it gets filed under luck or necessity or the way things go. The release is yours. You haven't signed it. Other people can see the hand that's moving and you can't.

Go earlier in the line and make one thing visible to yourself. Take something you're already setting down and do the one act that gets it outside your head — send the message, clear the shelf, settle the account. One act, today. It doesn't have to be big. It has to be yours in the daylight. What's already moving moves better once you can see your own hand on it.
cells.sheetLine: The release is yours, filed under the way things go.

attempts.check: The record supports the seat, the card, and the four mechanisms; what it does not support is any particular story about what the person is releasing, for whom, or how long they have held it — the draft keeps every reference to the release unnamed and to the moment recognizable rather than explained. A reasonable reader could say the Too Little cell locates a person behind the present, but the record's own tense for that status is past-anchored, so the cell names only where they are standing, never what happened there. The asks survive a wrong read because each one is the medicine's own act done small and teaches something even if the status is off; the sentence that serves me rather than them is any line that admires the steadiness of the release instead of handing it back, so those are cut. The four asks open on four verbs — give, hold, feed, cut — and none of them repeats the plan's phrasing five words in a row on the glass.
